Chapter 10: Delay

This chapter adds a fixed pause before each pipeline attempt continues. You will register and configure the Delay Controller, then observe that it changes execution timing without changing the candidate State.

The service owns the configuration and the component owns only the editor, feedback, and teaching display. An elapsed timer makes the pause visible without implementing the controller behavior.

Control when an accepted update proceeds, without changing the update.

Some State transitions need a deliberate pause: a UI transition may need time to settle, a loading experience may need realistic latency, or an external timing constraint may require a controlled handoff. This chapter adds that pause while preserving the candidate itself and the order of pipeline work.

Why this boundary matters

The Delay Controller owns when a pipeline attempt continues; the service owns configuration and State; the component only presents the elapsed experience. A delay is not debounce or throttle: every attempt still proceeds after the interval, and no candidate is transformed, collapsed, or discarded to create the timing effect.

Use this structure for

  • coordinating a visible State transition with a UI animation
  • simulating network latency while developing loading behavior
  • staging pipeline execution against an external timing constraint

By the end of this chapter

You will have a registered Delay Controller, a service-configured interval, and a visual elapsed-time indicator that proves each add, edit, or delete attempt pauses before the unchanged candidate commits.

Chapter 10 Starting Point and Timing Decision

Start with the completed Chapter 7 project. If your checkpoint does not already include , install it once. This chapter changes app.config.ts, the service, component, template, timing helper, and their tests.

Delay Changes Time, Not Meaning

The configured value is a fixed interval in milliseconds. The controller holds a pipeline attempt and later releases the same candidate. It does not debounce repeated attempts, throttle a stream, or choose a winning value.

Do Not Add Latency for Presentation Alone

Prefer CSS or Angular animation lifecycle APIs when only a visual effect must finish. Use pipeline delay when the State transition itself has an explicit timing requirement, or temporarily to simulate latency while developing loading behavior. Document the latency cost and verify the controller's queueing behavior before using overlapping requests.

Step 1: Configure the Delay Controller
↑ top

This step adds time-based execution control to the same service-owned character collection. The Delay Controller pauses each pipeline attempt for a fixed interval before allowing it to continue. It does not inspect, transform, filter, merge, reorder, or discard the candidate State.

Register withDelayController when you provide the , then configure the interval through withDelay() in example.service.ts. Keep that configuration in the service so the component remains responsible for presentation and user interaction while the service owns the boundary.

A fixed delay is useful when a State transition needs controlled timing. You might use it to coordinate a UI transition or animation, simulate network latency while developing a loading experience, stage a visible State change, or align pipeline execution with an external timing constraint. In each case, the Delay Controller pauses execution without changing which candidate State is processed.

Step 2: Update the Component and HTML for Delay
↑ top

The completed example makes the pause visible beside the character editor. Start an add, edit, or delete request and watch the elapsed value increase while the Delay Controller holds the pipeline attempt. When the interval expires, the attempt continues and the committed State updates.

In this example, example.elapsed-timer.ts is only a teaching helper. It measures wall-clock time with animation frames and publishes that measurement to the component so you can see the controller's hold interval. A real application would not use this helper to implement delay behavior or to decide when State may continue. The Delay Controller owns the pause and release decision. The helper does not represent a production timing service; it exists only for display purposes.

The component observes the service's State emissions to start and stop that display timer. It does not pause the pipeline, subscribe to a candidate source, or mutate committed State. The service and remain responsible for execution and State.

Supporting Elapsed Timer File

The example.elapsed-timer.ts contains the helper logic for managing the elapsed timer process.

This file is intentionally separate so the service stays minimal and the chapter stays focused on the state boundary instead of helper logic.

Troubleshooting the Timer

The elapsed value is display instrumentation, not the source of truth for pipeline timing. If its displayed duration varies slightly, verify the committed State transition and configured interval first. Browser frame scheduling can make a visual timer imprecise without changing controller behavior.

Rapid-Request Contract

The Delay Controller stores queued traces by trace ID. Each first attempt receives its own configured delay and is denied until its release time; expired traces are revoted and removed when allowed to continue. Reset or destroy clears queued traces and the active timer. This is delay, not debounce, cancellation, retry, or conflict resolution. 

t=0 ms    Request A denied and queued for t=1000
t=200 ms  Request B denied and queued for t=1200
t≈1000    Request A becomes eligible for revote
t≈1200    Request B becomes eligible for revote

Each trace receives its own deadline. Eligibility time is not a transactional or business-ordering guarantee.

What to Look For
  • Every update attempt is delayed; no attempt is debounced, collapsed, or dropped.
  • The elapsed timer is presentation-only and does not determine when the pipeline resumes.
  • The candidate continues through the configured pipeline unchanged after the delay expires.
  • The timer stops when the pipeline finalizes or enters Error State.
Chapter Round-up
↑ top

The Delay Controller chapter is complete when the example registers the controller, configures a fixed interval, and demonstrates that each update attempt pauses before the same candidate continues through the pipeline. The character collection still uses the service-owned boundary from the earlier workflow.

The important result is a clear ownership boundary. The controller owns timing, the service owns pipeline configuration and State updates, and the component owns the editor, feedback, and elapsed-time display. The example.elapsed-timer.ts file remains a display helper only; removing it would remove the visual measurement, not the Delay Controller behavior.

Run and Verify
  1. Confirm that the configured interval appears in the interactive example.
  2. Add or edit a character and verify that the elapsed display tracks the pause before the committed collection changes.
  3. In the final checkpoint, confirm that only withDelay() configures the pause. Removing example.elapsed-timer.ts would remove the display but would not change controller timing.
